deferredTracks.mechanism: A family of targeted statutes, each with its own form and rules: G.S. 15A-145 for offenses committed under age 18 or under 21 and for larceny by anyone; G.S. 15A-145.1 for gang offenses committed before age 18; G.S. 15A-145.2 and 15A-145.3 for certain drug conditional discharges; and G.S. 15A-145.4 for a nonviolent felony committed before age 18. Sequencing matters: an expunction under G.S. 15A-146 may bar later relief under G.S. 15A-145.4, while a person may obtain relief under G.S. 15A-145 before or simultaneously with G.S. 15A-146, because 15A-145 does not treat a 15A-146 expunction as a bar.

deferredTracks.publicName: A felony that is now a misdemeanor
deferredTracks.legalDesignRationale: Additional research required, as counsel decided, and high value: it converts ineligible participants into eligible ones. Reading § 12-1.3-1(5) at the official source closed counsel's first build blocker — the definition and the 26 June 2024 effective date are confirmed verbatim — but the two questions that make the overlay usable remain open: which offences the General Assembly has actually reclassified, which needs a maintained list, and whether reclassification lifts the no-felony-conviction bar in the multiple-misdemeanor route or only recharacterises the target offence. The track is deferred, absent from runtime resolution and unreachable, with counsel's structure preserved and the statutory confirmation recorded.
deferredTracks.mechanism: Section 12-1.3-1(5) provides that 'misdemeanor' includes, but is not limited to, those crimes previously classified as felonies under law at the time the original sentence was imposed but reclassified by the general assembly as a misdemeanor in the interim, prior to the time the motion to expunge is brought. A participant whose old conviction was a felony when imposed but is a misdemeanor today is therefore treated as a misdemeanant for expungement purposes, which moves them from the ten-year felony wait to the five-year misdemeanor wait and may make them eligible for the multiple-misdemeanor route they would otherwise be excluded from by the no-felony-conviction condition. This is an overlay on the first-offender misdemeanor and multiple-misdemeanor routes rather than a standalone remedy, and it is separated here because it has its own authority, its own effective date and its own factual test.

Reading § 23A-27-53 at the official source confirmed the mechanism and added two eligibility facts, but it did not answer the question that matters for record clearing: what record remains once the original charge is dismissed and the defendant stands convicted of the lesser ingestion or possession offence. The mechanism is a plea-bargaining structure rather than a record-clearing one, and its interaction with the arrest and SIS tracks is not established. The track is deferred, absent from runtime resolution and unreachable, with counsel's structure preserved.
deferredTracks.mechanism: After receiving a plea of guilty for a violation of § 22-42-5 or § 22-42-5.1 a court may, without entering a judgment of guilt and with the consent of the defendant, defer imposition of sentence and place the defendant on probation on terms that must include a drug and alcohol evaluation and any recommended course of treatment. If after one year the defendant has completed treatment and complied with all conditions, the court shall dismiss the § 22-42-5 or § 22-42-5.1 charge upon the defendant pleading guilty to ingestion under § 22-42-15 or possession under § 22-42-15.1. No person previously granted a deferred imposition of sentence is eligible for a second. A defendant is ineligible where aggravating circumstances exist as defined by § 22-6-11, or where the defendant is serving a sentence under the supervision of the executive branch.

deferredTracks.legalDesignRationale: Additional research required, as counsel decided. Reading § 23-6-8.1 at the official source answers counsel's question about whether destruction is automatic, discretionary or on request — the director 'may authorize' it, so it is discretionary and bureau-initiated with no participant application described — and it widens the section beyond the misdemeanor branch the review carried. deferredTracks.mechanism: The director of the Bureau of Criminal Statistics may authorize the destruction of information and records of: persons who are dead; persons seventy-five years of age or older unless a violation has occurred within the last ten years; incidents that are no longer considered crimes under the laws of South Dakota; and misdemeanor offenses whose final date of disposition occurred at least ten years prior to the authorized destruction date. Information and records received by the bureau may not be destroyed except as provided by this section. This is the only true destruction provision identified in South Dakota and it sits entirely outside the expungement chapter.

unresolvedQuestions.question: Counsel flagged as a release blocker whether § 23-6-8.1 destruction is automatic, discretionary or on request, because it determines whether there is anything for a participant to do. The section has now been read at the official South Dakota Legislature publication: the director of the Bureau of Criminal Statistics 'may authorize' the destruction. It is discretionary and bureau-initiated, and the section describes no participant application, petition or request. The section also covers three categories the review did not carry: deceased persons, persons seventy-five or older absent a violation in the last ten years, and incidents no longer considered crimes.

deferredTracks.publicName: Charges dismissed under a deferred prosecution agreement
deferredTracks.legalDesignRationale: Additional research required, as counsel decided. Reading § 967.055(3) at source sharpened the exclusion from a general 'OWI offense' bar into a specific enumerated list, but it did not identify the general adult deferred prosecution authority, did not establish whether dismissal terms vary across county programmes, and did not establish whether the resulting record clears the DOJ all-charges-cleared screen. The track is deferred, absent from runtime resolution and unreachable, with counsel's structure preserved.
deferredTracks.mechanism: Wisconsin prosecutors run deferred prosecution programmes at county level. A charge dismissed under such an agreement is a non-conviction and routes to DOJ fingerprint removal. Section 967.055(3) provides that a prosecutor may not place a person in a deferred prosecution programme where the person is accused of or charged with a violation of § 346.63(1) or (5) or a local ordinance in conformity therewith, a violation of § 346.63(2) or (6), or a violation of § 940.09 where the offense involved the use of a vehicle. The general adult deferred prosecution authority was not pinned, and dismissal terms may vary by county programme.
